root.text.Part 1.Chapter 2.0: A man of science made to me, several years ago, a remarkable objection that merits consideration, as well as the response we made to destroy it.
root.text.Part 1.Chapter 2.1: But before reporting the objection and the manner of destroying it, here is what I have to say. Every Hebrew knows that the name of [[t:0]]Élohîm[[t:1]] ([[t:2]]אלהים[[t:3]]) is homonymous, applying to God, angels, and rulers governing states. Already Onkelos, the proselyte, has explained, — and his explanation is true, — that by the words: [[t:4]]And you shall be as [[t:5]]Élohîm [[t:6]]knowing good and evil[[t:7]] (Genesis, 3, 5), the last sense was intended; for he says (in his Chaldaic translation): 'And you shall be as the [[t:8]]great personages[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]כרברביא[[t:11]]).'
root.text.Part 1.Chapter 2.2: Following this preliminary observation on the homonymy of this name, we shall report the objection.
root.text.Part 1.Chapter 2.3: It would appear, from the literal sense of the text, said the author of the objection, that the primitive intention in (the creation of) man was that he should be like the rest of the animals, without intellect and without reflection, and without the ability to distinguish between good and evil; but that, having disobeyed, his disobedience merited for him this great particular perfection of man, namely to possess this discernment which is in us, which is the most noble thing of our existence and which constitutes our substance. But it is a remarkable thing that his punishment for his disobedience should have been to give him a perfection which he had not previously possessed, namely, the intellect. It is absolutely similar to the assertion of those who have said that a certain man, after having disobeyed (God) and committed excesses of injustice, was transformed and placed as a star in the heaven[[fn:0]].—Such was the purpose and thought of the objection, although it was not (presented) in the same terms.
root.text.Part 1.Chapter 2.4: Hear now in what manner we have responded. O thou, we said, who examine [the things] with a superficial and unreflective intellect [[fn:1]], and who believest thou understandest a book, guide of the ancients and the moderns, by perusing it in a few moments of leisure [stolen from the pleasures] of drink and cohabitation, as one would peruse some historical book or poem! stop and examine; for the thing is not such as thou believedst at first sight, but such as it shall manifest itself when we have considered what I am about to say. The reason which God hath caused to emanate upon man, and which constitutes his final perfection, is that which Adam possessed before his disobedience; it is for this that it was said of him that he was [made] [[t:0]]to the image of God and to His likeness[[t:1]], and it is on account of this that the word was addressed to him and that he received commands, as it is said [in Scripture]: [[t:2]]And the Lord God commanded[[t:3]], etc. (Genesis, 2, 16), for one cannot give commands to animals nor to him who hath no reason. By reason one distinguisheth between the [[t:4]]true[[t:5]] and the [[t:6]]false[[t:7]], and this faculty he (Adam) possessed perfectly and completely; but the [[t:8]]ugly[[t:9]] and the [[t:10]]beautiful[[t:11]] exist in the [things of] [[t:12]]probable opinions[[t:13]], and not in the [[t:14]]intelligible things[[t:15]][[fn:2]]; for one does not say that this proposition: [[t:16]]the heaven is spherical[[t:17]], is beautiful, nor that this other: [[t:18]]the earth is flat[[t:19]], is ugly; but one calleth the one [[t:20]]true[[t:21]] and the other [[t:22]]false[[t:23]]. Thus in our language we employ (in speaking) of the [[t:24]]true[[t:25]] and the [[t:26]]false[[t:27]] (the words) [[t:28]]émeth[[t:29]] ([[t:30]]אמת[[t:31]]) and [[t:32]]schéker[[t:33]] ([[t:34]]שקר[[t:35]]), and for [[t:36]]beautiful[[t:37]] and [[t:38]]ugly[[t:39]] (we say) [[t:40]]tôb[[t:41]] ([[t:42]]טוב[[t:43]]) and [[t:44]]ra’[[t:45]] ([[t:46]]רע[[t:47]]). By reason, therefore, man distinguisheth the [[t:48]]true[[t:49]] from the [[t:50]]false[[t:51]], and this taketh place in all [Lat.: intelligibilia] intelligible things. When, therefore, he (Adam) was still in his most perfect and complete state, having only his primitive nature and his intelligible notions, on account of which it was said of him: [[t:52]]And Thou hast placed him a little lower than the divine beings[[t:53]] (Ps. 8, 6), there was in him no faculty which applied to the [[t:54]]probable opinions[[t:55]] in any manner, and he did not even comprehend them; so that what is most manifestly base with regard to the [[t:56]]probable opinions[[t:57]], that is to say, to discover the shameful parts, was not base to him, and he did not even comprehend its baseness. But when, disobeying, he inclined towards his desires coming from the imaginative and towards the bodily pleasures of his senses, as it is said (in Scripture): … [[t:58]]That the tree was good to eat and that it was a pleasure for the eyes[[t:59]] (Genesis, 3, 6), he was punished by the privation of this intellectual understanding; this is why he transgressed[[fn:3]] the order which had been given to him on account of his reason, and, having obtained the knowledge of the [[t:60]]probable opinions[[t:61]], he was absorbed by what he ought to have found base or beautiful, and he then knew what the thing was worth which had escaped him and of which he had been deprived, and in what state he had fallen. This is why it has been said: [[t:62]]And you shall be like Élohîm knowing good and evil[[t:63]] ([[t:64]]Ibid.[[t:65]], 3, 5), and one has not said: knowing the [[t:66]]false[[t:67]] and the [[t:68]]true[[t:69]], or: understanding the [[t:70]]false[[t:71]] and the [[t:72]]true;[[t:73]] whereas in the (domain of the) [[t:74]]necessary[[t:75]][[fn:4]] there is not at all good or evil, but false and true. — Consider also these words: [[t:76]]And the eyes of both of them were opened and they[[t:77]] [[t:78]]RECOGNIZED[[t:79]] [[t:80]]that they were naked[[t:81]] ([[t:82]]Ibid.[[t:83]], 3, 7). One does not say: And the eyes of both of them were opened and they [[t:84]]saw;[[t:85]] for what (man) had [[t:86]]seen[[t:87]] before, he also [[t:88]]saw[[t:89]] after. It is not that there was a veil on the eye which was then removed; but he underwent another state in which he found base what he had not found base before.
root.text.Part 1.Chapter 2.5: Be aware that this word, namely [[t:0]]פקח[[t:1]], is employed absolutely in the sense of: [[t:2]]opening the moral view[[t:3]] (and is not spoken of in relation to the rebirth of the sense of sight); for example: [[t:4]]And God opened his eyes[[t:5]] (Genesis, 21, 19); [[t:6]]Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened[[t:7]] (Isaiah, 35, 5); [[t:8]]Having opened ears, they do not hear[[t:9]] ([[t:10]]Ibid.[[t:11]], 42, 20), which resembles these words: [[t:12]]Those who have eyes to see and do not see[[t:13]] (Ezek., 12, 2).
root.text.Part 1.Chapter 2.6: With regard to that which is stated concerning Adam: [[t:0]]When he changed his[[t:1]] face [[t:2]]you sent him away[[t:3]] (Job, 14, 20)[[fn:5]], it must be interpreted and commented thus: 'When he changed his [[t:4]]direction[[t:5]] he was expelled'; for [[t:6]]פנים[[t:7]] (face, visage) is a noun derived from [[t:8]]פנה[[t:9]] (to turn), because man directs himself with his face towards the thing he wishes to attain. It is said, therefore: When he changed his direction and turned towards the thing towards which he had been previously forbidden to turn, he was expelled from paradise. And this was a punishment similar to his disobedience, [[t:10]]measure for measure[[t:11]][[fn:6]]; for he had been permitted to eat pleasant things and to delight in rest and tranquillity; but having become avid, having followed his pleasures and his imagination, as we have said, and having eaten that which had been forbidden to him, he was deprived of all and forced to eat that which was most vile in terms of food and that which had not served as his nourishment before, (and this still) with great toil and fatigue, as [Lat.: Scriptura] says: [[t:12]]She shall make you bring forth thorns and thistles, etc., by the sweat of your brow, etc.[[t:13]] (Genesis, 3, 18, 19), and then it is said clearly: [[t:14]]And the Lord God sent him away from paradise to cultivate the earth[[t:15]] ([[t:16]]Ibid.[[t:17]], [[t:18]]V[[t:19]]. 23). And He assimilated him to the animals in his food and in most circumstances, as [Lat.: Scriptura] says: [[t:20]]And you shall eat the herb of the field[[t:21]] ([[t:22]]Ibid.[[t:23]], [[t:24]]V[[t:25]]. 18). And as if to explain this passage (the psalmist) said: Man shall not remain in his dignity, and he was assimilated to the dumb beasts (Ps. 49, 13).
root.text.Part 1.Chapter 2.7: —Praise to the master of this will whose ultimate term and wisdom one cannot comprehend.
